questions.q: In which region did the Paharias primarily live, and what was their main mode of subsistence in the early 19th century?
questions.a: The Paharias lived around the Rajmahal hills (present-day Jharkhand/West Bengal border) and subsisted on shifting cultivation (jhum) using hoes, supplemented by forest produce like mahua, silk cocoons, resin, and charcoal. A wrong answer (e.g., "they were settled plough cultivators in the Gangetic plains") reveals the student confuses the Paharias with the Santhals or settled ryots, missing the fundamental contrast between hoe-based shifting cultivation and plough-based settled agriculture that drives the chapter's central conflict.

questions.q: Why did the British initially pursue a policy of "extermination" against the Paharias in the 1770s, and why did they switch to "pacification" by the 1780s?
questions.a: The British viewed Paharia raids on settled plains as a threat to revenue expansion and ordered extermination. When military suppression failed — Paharias retreated deeper into hills and continued raiding — Collector Augustus Cleveland introduced pacification: annual allowances to chiefs in exchange for maintaining order. A wrong answer (e.g., "the British wanted to civilise the Paharias by force") misses the pragmatic revenue motive: extermination was costly and ineffective; pacification was a cheaper way to secure the expanding agricultural frontier. The student who cites only "humanitarian reasons" ignores the colonial state's fiscal imperatives.

questions.q: Buchanan's 1810-11 survey describes the Paharias as "hostile, apprehensive of officials and unwilling to talk." Using the historical context, explain why the Paharias reacted this way to Buchanan's arrival.
questions.a: The Paharias' hostility stemmed from three decades of brutal repression (1770s extermination) followed by a pacification policy that co-opted their chiefs as stipendiary employees, eroding their authority. By 1810, every white official represented a power that had destroyed their way of life, seized forest control, and enabled Santhal encroachment on their lower hill territories. Buchanan's large entourage (surveyors, draughtsmen, coolies) looked like an invading army. A wrong answer (e.g., "they were naturally savage and hostile to all outsiders") reproduces the colonial stereotype Buchanan himself held, ignoring the specific historical trauma of extermination, broken treaties, and land loss that shaped Paharia perception.

questions.q: Compare the ecological requirements of Paharia shifting cultivation with Santhal plough agriculture. How did the creation of Damin-i-Koh (1832) disrupt the Paharias' subsistence cycle?
questions.a: Paharia jhum required mobility: clearing patches, burning for potash, cultivating 2-3 years, then leaving land fallow 10-15 years to recover fertility — needing vast forest territory. Santhal plough agriculture required permanent fields, clearing forests irreversibly. Damin-i-Koh demarcated the lower fertile hills as Santhal territory, legally barring Paharias from the very lands their fallow cycle depended on. Confined to rocky upper hills with thin soil, Paharias could not sustain shifting cultivation. A wrong answer (e.g., "both were farmers so they could share the land") fails to grasp that the two systems were ecologically incompatible: one needs forest rotation, the other needs permanent clearance. The student who misses the "fallow cycle" concept cannot explain why displacement to upper hills was catastrophic.

questions.q: The NCERT text states: "To the British, extension of settled agriculture was necessary to enlarge the sources of land revenue... They also associated forests with wildness, and saw forest people as savage, unruly, primitive, and difficult to govern." Evaluate whether this ideological framing was a cause or a justification for colonial policy toward the Paharias.
questions.a: It was both cause and justification, operating in a feedback loop. The revenue imperative (cause) drove forest clearance; the "savage/primitive" label (justification) legitimised dispossession by portraying Paharias as obstacles to progress. Cleveland's pacification already assumed Paharias needed to be "tamed" into plough cultivators. When Santhals proved more amenable to settled agriculture, the ideology reinforced the policy shift. A wrong answer (e.g., "it was just an excuse; the real reason was revenue") oversimplifies: ideology shaped *how* revenue was extracted (e.g., preferring Santhal settlers over Paharia chiefs). The student who separates "ideology" from "material interest" misses how colonial knowledge production served power.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (1770-1832) showing the major turning points in British-Paharia relations and the arrival of Santhals, then write a 3-sentence historical argument explaining the Paharias' long-term marginalisation.
questions.a: Timeline: 1770s — British extermination policy; 1780s — Cleveland's pacification (allowances to chiefs); 1800 — Santhals begin arriving in Rajmahal; 1810-11 — Buchanan's survey (Paharias hostile, withdrawing); 1832 — Damin-i-Koh demarcated for Santhals; 1838-1851 — Santhal villages grow from 40 to 1,473. Argument: The Paharias were marginalised not by a single act but by a structural shift: colonial revenue logic privileged sedentary plough agriculture over mobile shifting cultivation, and the Santhals became the instrument of that transformation. Paharia resistance (raids, withdrawal) was met with military force then co-option, but the ecological basis of their autonomy — access to vast forested hills for fallow rotation — was legally and physically erased by the Damin-i-Koh settlement. A poor answer lists dates without linking them to the causal chain (revenue → forest clearance → Santhal settlement → Paharia displacement).

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Paharias were a tribal community inhabiting the Rajmahal hills (present-day Jharkhand) in the late 18th and early 19th centuries who practised shifting cultivation (jhum) using hoes, gathered forest produce (mahua, silk cocoons, resin), and ______ raided the plains.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing in the Rajmahal hills today — the forests are thinner, the hills scarred by old ______ patches.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the ecological and economic logic of Paharia shifting cultivation, contrast British extermination and pacification policies with their outcomes, and analyse how the expansion of plough agriculture (Santhal settlement) and colonial revenue imperatives led to the Paharias' marginalisation, using specific evidence.
